Reproducing Pasquereau & Turner (2013) from dandiset 001636¶

Paper: Pasquereau B, Turner RS (2013). Primary motor cortex of the parkinsonian monkey: altered neuronal responses to muscle stretch. Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience 7:98. doi:10.3389/fnsys.2013.00098. The claims file was written from the full text (open access, PubMed Central PMC3840326) and its supplementary data sheet, whose table gives the neuronal results of each monkey separately.

Dandiset: DANDI:001636, version draft, as asked for this attempt. The draft was last modified on 2026-10-21 at 20:16:41 UTC (the first cell prints the modification time read at run time); a draft can change, and when it was read the archive listed 4 uploads in progress. Between 23:00 and 23:10 UTC on the same day every asset of the draft was uploaded again; this run read the draft after that (the first cell prints the time), and every number recorded from the earlier state (the attempt record and the conclusions) is unchanged. This is a repeat attempt: the earlier one, 001636-pasquereau-2013-01, used the published version 0.260518.1819. Since then the files were reconverted to fix what that attempt found, and the fixes are not yet published, so the draft is tested here. The paper (2013) cites no DANDI version.

How the draft differs from 0.260518.1819, in what the analysis uses (shown in the data check): it holds 439 files where the published version held 447. Source files recorded on the same day and linked through a neuron recorded across them are merged into one session, and a unit is observed only in the trials of its own source files (its obs_intervals), so each unit's perturbations are counted within those trials. The merge adds trials of second files that the published version did not hold (for 12 monkey V units), and removes the four files that repeated another file's trials and the two unit copies they held. The analog streams now share the clock of the trials, the angle's reference frame says positive is flexion, the monkey L series are named WristAngle and WristTorque, unit_name gives the source file and unit (v2701.1+v2702.2), and unit_also_in_session_id is gone. The monkey L perturbation type is not_available where it was none. Every file was replaced; the angle, torque command and triceps EMG values compared in one file (v4527) while preparing are unchanged (not run here).

What can be tested. The files of monkey V (Venus, elbow) mark the torque perturbations, with the joint angle, the torque command and triceps EMG. The files of monkey L (Leu, wrist) mark none, so every claim is tested on monkey V alone, against the paper's monkey V values where it gives them (supplementary table) and against its pooled values otherwise.

Claim Tested
cell-counts: 112 and 159 monkey V cells, 49 and 54 PTNs, 31 and 48 CSNs, 3 dual yes
monkey-l-perturbations: monkey L torque responses blocked (data missing)
baseline-rate: lower resting rate after MPTP in PTNs, not CSNs yes
ptn-faster-than-csn: PTNs fire faster than CSNs before MPTP yes
antidromic-latency: CSN antidromic latency longer after MPTP, PTN unchanged yes
false-positive-rate: the detection threshold's false-positive rate near 0.01 run, blocked (methods underspecified)
torque-related-fractions: monkey V fractions of torque-related cells run, blocked (methods underspecified)
prevalence-unchanged: MPTP does not change the fraction of torque-related cells run, blocked (methods underspecified)
ptn-more-responsive: PTNs respond more often than CSNs run, blocked (methods underspecified)
one-direction-half: 44% of torque-related cells respond to one direction only run, blocked (methods underspecified)
excitatory-majority: most responses are increases; PTN balance unchanged run, blocked (methods underspecified)
magnitude-unchanged: response magnitudes unchanged by MPTP run, blocked (methods underspecified)
venus-response-magnitudes: monkey V response magnitudes run, blocked (methods underspecified)
latency-shorter: response latencies shorter after MPTP run, blocked (methods underspecified)
latency-not-training: latencies do not follow days of training run, blocked (methods underspecified)
fwhm-shorter-ptn: PTN increases briefer after MPTP run, blocked (methods underspecified)
dsi-reduced: fewer directional responses after MPTP run, blocked (methods underspecified)
venus-dsi: monkey V mean DSI run, blocked (methods underspecified)
dsi-not-baseline: resting rate does not differ between directional categories run, blocked (methods underspecified)
kinematics-slower: torque-induced movements slower and smaller after MPTP yes
kinematic-latency-unchanged: movement latency unchanged yes
emg-m2-larger: larger long-latency (m2) triceps response after MPTP yes
emg-duration-longer: longer EMG responses after MPTP yes
emg-onset-unchanged: EMG onset unchanged yes
emg-m1-weak: m1 much smaller than m2 yes
velocity-matched-magnitude: magnitudes unchanged in velocity-matched sessions run, blocked (methods underspecified)
session-correlations: no session-level correlation of PTN latency with velocity or m2 run, blocked (methods underspecified)
trial-correlations: no trial-level correlation blocked (methods underspecified)

The detection's false-positive rate (false-positive-rate) is 0.23 here with the detection fixed in the claims file (0.46 with the t-test variant), far from the 0.01 the paper's threshold implies, so the procedure differs from the paper's and false-positive-rate is blocked with methods_underspecified. The claims file blocks the 15 claims that rest on the selection of responses for the same reason when that rate falls outside 0.0033 to 0.03. Their analyses are run all the same, and their numbers are reported for reference; none of them decides an outcome.

Code read. The paper links no analysis code. The dandiset links its conversion code, catalystneuro/turner-lab-to-nwb. Its main branch is still at commit e80a192917490b50db6871180b6d1d9a24772e35, read for the earlier attempt; the code that built the draft is in an open pull request, #33 (branch fix_errors, head 5f9bf6320a0160e4e56301d5409fb9242c1d8cf4), whose description was read: it merges linked source files into sessions, reads the second file of each neuron recorded across files, drops repeated trials, and lays the analog streams by trial. It holds no analysis of the torque responses, so every method choice here comes from the paper's Methods or is fixed in the claims file.

The claims, with their criteria, are in claims/001636/10.3389-fnsys.2013.00098.yaml. The loading and the measures are in stretch.py, whose docstring says which parameters come from the paper and which were chosen here.

The draft holds 439 files with 566 units: 210 of monkey L (Leu) and 356 of monkey V (Venus). The MPTP state in the session id agrees with each unit's is_post_mptp. Leu files date from August 1992 to December 1993, as the draft's description now says (earlier finding: the description said 1993 only; fixed).

Every Leu trial has the perturbation type not_available (it was none), so no monkey L trial can be identified as perturbed. The monkey V units with at least 5 perturbations of each direction within their own trials number 115 before and 157 after MPTP, with 51 and 54 PTNs and 32 and 48 CSNs. In the published version these counts were 112 and 159, 49 and 54, 31 and 48, the paper's supplementary table. Counting all perturbations of the session for each unit selects the same units. Thirteen units (12 of monkey V) are recorded across two source files; their spikes all fall inside their obs_intervals. The other projection types (thalamic and subthalamic projections) are counted as non-identified (NA) cells, as the paper has no such category, and the dual PTN and CSN units are kept apart from both.

old = pd.DataFrame(stretch.load_all_brief(stretch.asset_urls(stretch.EARLIER_VERSION)))
old["studied"] = (old.n_flex >= stretch.MIN_REPS) & (old.n_ext >= stretch.MIN_REPS)
old["ptype"] = old.type.map(stretch.short_type)
old["state"] = np.where(old.post, "post", "pre")
print(f"Version {stretch.EARLIER_VERSION}: {old.path.nunique()} files, {len(old)} units; this version: "
      f"{len(sessions)} files, {len(units)} units")
print(f"Files of {stretch.EARLIER_VERSION} not in this version:", sorted(set(old.path) - set(s["path"] for s in S)))
print(f"\nMonkey V cells studied in {stretch.EARLIER_VERSION}, by type and state:")
print(pd.crosstab(old[old.studied & (old.subject == "Venus")].ptype, old[old.studied & (old.subject == "Venus")].state)
      .reindex(columns=["pre", "post"]).to_string())
# match each old unit to the unit of this version that lists it in its unit_name
part_of = {p: n for n in units.unit_name for p in n.split("+")}
old["now"] = old.unit_name.map(part_of)
now = units.set_index("unit_name")
diff = []
for r in old[old.subject == "Venus"].itertuples():
    n = now.loc[r.now] if isinstance(r.now, str) else None
    row = {"unit_then": r.unit_name, "type_then": r.ptype, "studied_then": r.studied,
           "flex_ext_then": f"{r.n_flex}/{r.n_ext}", "unit_now": r.now if n is not None else "(absent)",
           "type_now": n.ptype if n is not None else "", "studied_now": bool(n.studied) if n is not None else False,
           "flex_ext_now": f"{n.n_flex}/{n.n_ext}" if n is not None else ""}
    if (row["type_then"], row["studied_then"], row["flex_ext_then"]) != (row["type_now"], row["studied_now"], row["flex_ext_now"]):
        diff.append(row)
print("\nMonkey V units whose type, perturbation counts or selection differ between the versions:")
print(pd.DataFrame(diff).to_string(index=False))

Against version 0.260518.1819, used by the earlier attempt: that version had 447 files and 568 units, and its selection gives the supplementary table's counts exactly (112 and 159 cells, 49 and 54 PTNs, 31 and 48 CSNs). The eight files it held that this version does not were second files of a neuron or repeats of another file's trials; their units are now in the sessions they continue. Twelve monkey V units gain the trials of their second file, which brings three of them (v1902.1, v2701.1 and v3607.1, two PTNs and a CSN, all before MPTP) to at least 5 perturbations of each direction. After MPTP, the two unit copies of repeated files (v4527b.2, a PTN, and v5812.2, labelled no_response) are gone, and v4527.2, labelled not_tested there, is now a PTN. These changes account for every difference in the counts of cells studied.

In monkey V the joint moves by more than 2 deg in the hold window in 67% (pre) and 86.5% (post) of perturbed trials and in 1% and 11% of the others. In monkey L it does so in 15% of trials before MPTP and 1% after, which does not fit perturbations on two thirds of the trials as the Methods describe; these windows were set from the monkey V onsets, so the monkey L perturbations could fall outside them. Either way, the monkey L torque trials cannot be identified from the files, and monkey-l-perturbations is blocked. The Leu torque command is NaN in every pre-MPTP file (98) and in one post-MPTP file, and 15 post-MPTP Leu files have no analog data. Earlier finding (no monkey L perturbations): still present in the data; the draft's description and the torque series now say that the Leu source files hold no perturbation times. The Leu analog streams are sampled at 100 Hz, where the paper says 200 Hz for monkey L; monkey V is sampled at 1 kHz (the paper digitized at 500 Hz; the conversion notes say the lab interpolated to 1 kHz).

# Every excursion of the torque command (more than 20 units from rest, lasting at least 10 ms),
# in every file with a torque command; a hold-period impulse starts in the hold window.
exc_rows = []
for s in S:
    if "command_excursions" not in s:
        continue
    e = s["command_excursions"]
    e = e[e.duration_ms >= 10]
    h = e[e.in_hold]
    exc_rows.append({"subject": s["subject"], "state": "post" if s["post"] else "pre", "code": s["session_id"].split("++")[1],
                     "trials": len(s["trials"]), "excursions": len(e),
                     "labelled_torque_trials": int(s["trials"].torque.isin(["flexion", "extension"]).sum()),
                     "trials_hold_excursion": h.trial.nunique(),
                     "trials_hold_40_70ms": h[(h.duration_ms >= 40) & (h.duration_ms <= 70)].trial.nunique(),
                     "hold_median_ms": h.duration_ms.median(), "hold_median_abs_peak": h.peak.abs().median(),

The torque command shows the same. In monkey V a command excursion starts in the hold window in 1882 pre-MPTP and 3517 post-MPTP trials, against 1947 and 3603 labelled perturbations; before MPTP every one of them lasts 40 to 70 ms. In monkey L the command is NaN in every pre-MPTP file, and 34 post-MPTP files hold one (35 in the published version, where l16301b was a file of its own). Of their 2048 trials, one has an excursion starting in the hold window (70 ms, 41 units). Their 88 to 767 excursions per file start a median 0.30 to 0.83 s after the lateral target appears, during the active movement. No monkey L file holds a hold-period torque impulse.

AX = np.arange(stretch.ANALOG_WINDOW_MS[0], stretch.ANALOG_WINDOW_MS[1] + 1)


def command_onset(w):
    # first ms where the torque command leaves its pre-onset level by more than 6 SD (and 10 units)
    base = np.nanmedian(w[:, :400], axis=1, keepdims=True)
    sd = np.nanstd(w[:, :400], axis=1, keepdims=True)
    dev = np.abs(w - base) > np.maximum(10, 6 * sd)
    return np.where(dev.any(1), AX[np.argmax(dev, axis=1)], np.nan)

lag = np.concatenate([s["analog_lag_ms"][s["pert_trial"]] for s in venus])
ok = np.isfinite(stored) & np.isfinite(realigned)

Earlier finding (analog clock): fixed. In the published version the analog streams were laid end to end by their sample count and fell behind the trials table by about 5 ms per trial, so the torque command step appeared up to 108 ms before the labelled onset. In the draft each analog segment starts at its trial's start: the lag stretch.realign would correct is 0 ms at every perturbation, and on the stored clock the command steps 4 to 6 ms (1st to 99th percentile) after the labelled onset, the same as after realignment. The EMG series share the angle's timestamps. Three sessions (v1401, v1402, v1501) have labelled perturbations but no step in the torque command, as the draft's torque description says; their 51 perturbations are kept (the command is not used to select trials).

Earlier finding (reference frame): fixed. The angle's reference_frame now says positive is flexion in every file with an angle, and the values agree: active flexion movements raise the angle by about 18 deg in both monkeys and extension movements lower it, and flexion torques raise it in 99.8% of perturbations. The monkey L series are now named WristAngle and WristTorque. The torque labels agree with the EMG (the triceps, an extensor stretched by a flexion torque, responds to flexion torques; see the EMG sections).

The angle's scale agrees with the files' own kinematic columns. Active movements measured here, with the filter used for the torque-evoked movements, have median peak velocities and amplitudes within 2% of derived_peak_velocity and derived_movement_amplitude (median ratios 0.99 to 1.02; Spearman rho 0.994 in monkey V and 0.989 in monkey L for peak velocity), and their median amplitude (20.4 deg in monkey V) matches the 20 deg targets. The angle is consistent with degrees, as stated, and the filter keeps the peak velocity of these movements.

# Spikes against the trials table: does the torque direction become decodable from single-cell
# spike counts only after the labelled onset? 20 ms windows, Mann-Whitney flexion vs extension.
edges = np.arange(-200, 201, 20)
studied_v = units[units.studied & (units.subject == "Venus")]
sig = np.zeros(len(edges) - 1)
for r in studied_v.itertuples():
    s, u = S[r.si], S[r.si]["units"][r.ui]
    counts = np.array([np.histogram(x, edges)[0] for x in u["pert"]])
    f, e = counts[u["pert_direction"] == "flexion"], counts[u["pert_direction"] == "extension"]
    for j in range(len(edges) - 1):
        if np.ptp(np.r_[f[:, j], e[:, j]]) > 0:
            sig[j] += stats.mannwhitneyu(f[:, j], e[:, j]).pvalue < 0.01
frac = sig / len(studied_v)
print(f"Fraction of the {len(studied_v)} monkey V cells studied whose spike counts differ between "
      "flexion and extension trials (Mann-Whitney p < 0.01), by window (ms from labelled onset):")
print(pd.Series(frac.round(3), index=[f"{a} to {b}" for a, b in zip(edges[:-1], edges[1:])]).to_string())

The spike times therefore share the trials table's clock to within the 20 ms windows, consistent with the 20 to 60 ms response latencies of the paper.

# Files that repeat another file's recording: same subject and date, and the trial durations of one
# are a contiguous block of the other's.
dur = {si: np.round((s["trials"].stop - s["trials"].start).values, 3) for si, s in enumerate(S)}
repeats = []
for (subj, date), g in sessions.groupby(["subject", "date"]):
    for a in g.si:
        for b in g.si:
            if a != b and len(dur[b]) <= len(dur[a]) and (len(dur[b]) < len(dur[a]) or a < b):
                n = len(dur[b])
                if any(np.array_equal(dur[a][i:i + n], dur[b]) for i in range(len(dur[a]) - n + 1)):
                    repeats.append({"file": sessions.code[a], "repeated_in": sessions.code[b],
                                    "trials": len(dur[a]), "repeated_trials": n,
                                    "units_file": [u["unit_name"] for u in S[a]["units"]],
                                    "units_repeat": [u["unit_name"] for u in S[b]["units"]],
                                    "types_file": [stretch.short_type(u["type"]) for u in S[a]["units"]],
                                    "types_repeat": [stretch.short_type(u["type"]) for u in S[b]["units"]]})
repeats = pd.DataFrame(repeats, columns=["file", "repeated_in", "trials", "repeated_trials", "units_file",
                                        "units_repeat", "types_file", "types_repeat"])
repeated_files = set(repeats.repeated_in)
print("Files whose trials repeat a block of another file's trials:", "none" if repeats.empty else "")
print(repeats.to_string(index=False))
# Within a merged session: does a later source file repeat trials of an earlier one?
within = []
for si, s in enumerate(S):
    tr = s["trials"]
    if tr.source_file.nunique() < 2:
        continue
    key = list(zip(np.round((tr.stop - tr.start).values, 3), tr.torque, tr.movement))
    files = tr.source_file.values
    first_file = {}
    for k, f in zip(key, files):
        first_file.setdefault(k, f)
    within.append({"session": sessions.code[si], "source_files": list(pd.unique(files)), "trials": len(tr),
                   "trials_repeating_an_earlier_file": sum(first_file[k] != f for k, f in zip(key, files))})
print("\nMerged sessions (several source files) and trials of a later file that repeat a trial of an earlier one "
      "(same duration, torque and movement):")
print(pd.DataFrame(within).to_string(index=False))


def trial_spikes(s, u):
    # spike times relative to the start of their trial, one array per trial
    tr = s["trials"]
    k = np.searchsorted(tr.start.values, u["spikes"], side="right") - 1
    return [np.round(u["spikes"][k == i] - tr.start.values[i], 4) for i in range(len(tr))]


same_unit = []
for r in repeats.itertuples():
    a = S[int(sessions[sessions.code == r.file].si.iloc[0])]
    b = S[int(sessions[sessions.code == r.repeated_in].si.iloc[0])]
    da, db = dur[int(sessions[sessions.code == r.file].si.iloc[0])], dur[int(sessions[sessions.code == r.repeated_in].si.iloc[0])]
    off = [i for i in range(len(da) - len(db) + 1) if np.array_equal(da[i:i + len(db)], db)][0]
    for ub in b["units"]:
        tb = trial_spikes(b, ub)
        for ua in a["units"]:
            ta = trial_spikes(a, ua)[off:off + len(db)]
            n_same = sum(np.array_equal(x, y) for x, y in zip(ta, tb))
            same_unit.append({"file": r.file, "unit": ua["unit_name"], "type": ua["type"],
                              "repeat": r.repeated_in, "repeat_unit": ub["unit_name"], "repeat_type": ub["type"],
                              "identical_trials": f"{n_same}/{len(db)}",
                              "spikes_in_block": (sum(map(len, ta)), sum(map(len, tb)))})
same_unit = pd.DataFrame(same_unit, columns=["file", "unit", "type", "repeat", "repeat_unit", "repeat_type",
                                          "identical_trials", "spikes_in_block"])
print("\nUnits of each repeated recording compared trial by trial over the repeated block:")
print(same_unit.to_string(index=False))
dup_units = same_unit[same_unit.identical_trials.str.split("/", regex=False).str[0].astype(int) > 0]
# the copy in the repeated file is the one dropped in the variant that counts each unit once
dup_keys = {(r.repeat, r.repeat_unit) for r in dup_units.itertuples()}
units["duplicate_copy"] = [(sess.split("++")[1], un) in dup_keys for sess, un in zip(units.session, units.unit_name)]
print("Unit copies in repeated files (dropped in the variant that counts each unit once):", sorted(dup_keys))

print("\nUnits with unit_also_in_session_id set:", int((units.also_in != "").sum()),
      "| files with the unit_also_in_session_id column:", sum(s["has_also_in_column"] for s in S), "of", len(S))
# Units recorded across several source files: their firing rate over the trials of each file, as a
# check that the parts are one neuron (spike times are only inside the unit's obs_intervals).
rows = []
for r in units[units.source_files > 1].itertuples():
    s, u = S[r.si], S[r.si]["units"][r.ui]
    tr = s["trials"][u["observed_trials"]]
    rates = {}
    for f, g in tr.groupby("source_file", sort=False):
        n = sum(int(((u["spikes"] >= a) & (u["spikes"] <= b)).sum()) for a, b in zip(g.start, g.stop))
        rates[f] = round(n / float((g.stop - g.start).sum()), 2)
    rows.append({"unit": r.unit_name, "subject": r.subject, "type": r.ptype, "studied": r.studied,
                 "rate_by_file (spikes/s)": rates})
merged_units = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(merged_units.to_string(index=False))
print("\nSpike times sorted in every unit:", bool(units["sorted"].all()),
      "| spikes outside the trials:", int(units.outside_trials.sum()))
print("Within-trial ISIs below 2 ms, fraction per unit: median "
      f"{units.isi_below_2ms.median():.4f}, units above 1%: {int((units.isi_below_2ms > 0.01).sum())} of {len(units)} "
      f"({int((units[units.studied & (units.subject == 'Venus')].isi_below_2ms > 0.01).sum())} of the cells studied)")

Spike times sorted in every unit: True | spikes outside the trials: 0
Within-trial ISIs below 2 ms, fraction per unit: median 0.0006, units above 1%: 68 of 566 (36 of the cells studied)

Earlier finding (repeated files and unit copies): fixed. No file repeats a block of another file's trials. The four repeated files of the published version (v4527b, v4810b, v5604b, v5812) are folded into the sessions they repeat, their repeated trials left out, and the two unit copies they held (v4527b.2 and v5812.2) are stored once, as v4527.2 and v5811.2, both PTNs; the files' notes say which projection label was kept and why. Within the 13 merged sessions, trials of a later file match no trial of an earlier one in monkey V; in l16301 one trial of 120 matches on duration and movement alone, which a coincidence explains as well as a repeat. The variants below that drop unit copies are kept from the earlier attempt; there is nothing left to drop, so they equal the main results.

Earlier finding (unit_also_in_session_id): fixed. The column is in none of the files. Units recorded across two source files are now one unit, named after both (v2701.1+v2702.2) and observed in the trials of both. Treating each as one cell is the dataset's statement, taken here as an assumption; their rates over the trials of each file differ by less than a factor of 1.5 in 8 of the 13, and by up to 3.2 (v3202.1+v3202b.1, 2.81 and 9.12 spikes/s). A variant of cell-counts counts each from its first file only.

Every unit's spike times are sorted and fall within the trials. The paper verified isolation by a refractory period over 2 ms; a few units have more than 1% of their ISIs below 2 ms (68 of 566, 36 of the cells studied), and they are kept, as the dandiset holds the units the paper selected.

emg_rows = []
for s in venus:
    for ch in stretch.EMG_CHANNELS[:3]:
        if ch not in s["windows"]:
            state = "absent"
        else:
            w = s["windows"][ch]
            if np.isnan(w).any():
                state = "NaN"
            elif np.nanstd(w[:, AX < 0]) < 1:
                state = "flat"
            else:
                state = "used"
        emg_rows.append({"code": s["session_id"].split("++")[1], "post": s["post"], "channel": ch, "state": state})
emg_avail = pd.DataFrame(emg_rows)
emg_avail["repeat"] = emg_avail.code.isin(repeated_files)
print("Monkey V triceps channels per file (repeated files excluded), by state:")
print(pd.crosstab([emg_avail[~emg_avail.repeat].channel], [emg_avail[~emg_avail.repeat].post, emg_avail[~emg_avail.repeat].state]).to_string())
vals = np.concatenate([s["windows"][ch].ravel() for s in venus for ch in stretch.EMG_CHANNELS[:3] if ch in s["windows"]])
print(f"\nTriceps EMG values (A/D units, as stored in a.u.): {np.nanmin(vals):.0f} to {np.nanmax(vals):.0f}, "
      f"median {np.nanmedian(vals):.0f}")
ang = np.concatenate([s["windows"]["angle"].ravel() for s in venus])
print(f"Monkey V angle around perturbations: {np.nanmin(ang):.1f} to {np.nanmax(ang):.1f} deg")
tq = np.concatenate([s["windows"]["torque_cmd"].ravel() for s in venus])
print(f"Monkey V torque command (arbitrary units): {np.nanmin(tq):.0f} to {np.nanmax(tq):.0f}")
iv = np.concatenate([(s["trials"].onset - s["trials"].center_on).dropna().values for s in venus])
# size of the torque command step (sign-corrected, 10 to 40 ms after onset, less the 100 ms before)
command = []
for s in venus:
    w = s["windows"]["torque_cmd"]
    sign = np.where(s["pert_direction"] == "flexion", 1.0, -1.0)[:, None]
    rel = (w - np.nanmedian(w[:, (AX >= -100) & (AX < 0)], axis=1, keepdims=True)) * sign
    m = np.nanmean(rel, axis=0)
    command.append({"session": s["session_id"], "code": s["session_id"].split("++")[1], "post": s["post"],
                    "date": s["date"], "step": float(np.nanmedian(rel[:, (AX >= 10) & (AX < 40)])),
                    "width_ms": int((m > m.max() / 2).sum()), "after_pulse": float(m[(AX >= 70) & (AX < 150)].mean())})
command = pd.DataFrame(command)
command["level"] = np.round(command.step / command.step[command.step > 10].min()).astype(int)
print("\nTorque command step (units above the pre-onset level) by state; level = step in multiples of the smallest:")
print(pd.crosstab(command.level, command.post).to_string())
print(command.groupby(["post", "level"])[["step", "width_ms", "after_pulse"]].median().round(1).to_string())
# per-trial step, against the level of its session
trial_steps = []
for s, lv in zip(venus, command.level):
    w = s["windows"]["torque_cmd"]
    sign = np.where(s["pert_direction"] == "flexion", 1.0, -1.0)
    rel = (w - np.nanmedian(w[:, (AX >= -100) & (AX < 0)], axis=1, keepdims=True)) * sign[:, None]
    step = np.nanmedian(rel[:, (AX >= 10) & (AX < 40)], axis=1)
    trial_steps.append(pd.DataFrame({"post": s["post"], "session_level": lv,
                                     "trial_level": np.round(step / command.step[command.step > 10].min())}))
trial_steps = pd.concat(trial_steps, ignore_index=True)
print("Per-trial step in multiples of the smallest level, against its session's level (perturbations):")
print(pd.crosstab([trial_steps.post, trial_steps.session_level], trial_steps.trial_level).to_string())
print("Dates of the level-2 sessions by state:", command[command.level == 2].groupby("post").date.agg(["min", "max", "count"]).to_string())
print("Torque onset after the center target appears (s), percentiles 0/5/50/95/100:",
      np.percentile(iv, [0, 5, 50, 95, 100]).round(3))

EMG units are A/D values stored as arbitrary units, so EMG is compared only within the dandiset. Earlier finding (sampling and EMG description): partly fixed. The EMG description now gives the paper's processing (rectified and low-pass filtered at 100 Hz) where it said sample-hold integrated over 10 ms; the values are the same as in the published version (checked on v4527 while preparing, not run here). The A/D units and the 100 Hz monkey L sampling remain, and the draft's description now states both.

Earlier finding (torque command sizes): partly fixed. The data are unchanged: the command's 50 ms pulse has three session sizes, about 46, 91 and 183 units above rest; 105 of 154 pre-MPTP sessions have the smallest and 125 of 137 post-MPTP sessions the largest, with the middle size in 43 and 12 sessions, and post-MPTP pulses are followed by an opposite swing of about 30 to 37 units. Within post-MPTP sessions the step also varies from trial to trial (1 to 8 times the smallest level in the sessions of the largest size). The torque description now says all this, and that no conversion to newton-metres is available, so whether the torque or only the command's scaling changed still cannot be told. The paper says every impulse was 0.1 Nm for 50 ms. The pre and post perturbations are not shown to be the same; the kinematic and EMG claims add a variant restricted to sessions of the middle size, which both states have.

Earlier finding (torque timing): still present, now described. The torque onset follows the appearance of the center target by 1.696 to 1.732 s in 90% of monkey V perturbations (5th to 95th percentile). The Methods put it 1 to 2 s, uniformly at random, after the monkey captured the center target; the draft's description now states the difference. This does not enter any analysis here.

Responses of the cells studied¶

Every monkey V cell studied is analysed once, below, and the claims draw on these tables. For each cell: the single-trial SDFs (causal gamma kernel, k = 1.5, theta = 20 ms), its baseline rate (mean SDF over the 500 ms before onset, all perturbations), and for each direction the response found by the main detection (threshold on the trial-averaged SDF) and by the variant (t-test across trials), at the true onset and at a pseudo onset 600 ms earlier.

cells = units[units.studied & (units.subject == "Venus")].copy().reset_index(drop=True)
resp_rows, base, mean_sdf = [], [], {}
for c in cells.itertuples():
    s, u = S[c.si], S[c.si]["units"][c.ui]
    X = stretch.sdfs(u["pert"])
    base.append(X[:, stretch._mask(*stretch.BASELINE_MS)].mean())
    for d in ("flexion", "extension"):
        Xd = X[u["pert_direction"] == d]
        mean_sdf[(c.Index, d)] = Xd.mean(0)
        for method, shift in (("mean", 0), ("trials", 0), ("mean", stretch.PSEUDO_ONSET_MS),
                              ("trials", stretch.PSEUDO_ONSET_MS)):
            r = stretch.detect(Xd, shift_ms=shift, method=method)
            r.update(cell=c.Index, direction=d, method=method, pseudo=shift != 0)
            resp_rows.append(r)
cells["baseline_rate"] = base
R = pd.DataFrame(resp_rows).merge(cells[["state", "ptype", "si", "date", "duplicate_copy"]],
                                  left_on="cell", right_index=True)
main = R[(R.method == "mean") & ~R.pseudo]
by_cell = main.pivot(index="cell", columns="direction")
cells["torque_related"] = by_cell["responds"].any(axis=1).values
cells["n_directions"] = by_cell["responds"].sum(axis=1).values
cells["latency"] = by_cell["latency"].min(axis=1).values
dsis = [stretch.dsi(main[(main.cell == i) & (main.direction == "flexion")].iloc[0].to_dict(),
                    main[(main.cell == i) & (main.direction == "extension")].iloc[0].to_dict())
        for i in cells.index]
cells["dsi"] = [d for d, _ in dsis]
cells["category"] = [c for _, c in dsis]
resp = main[main.responds].copy()
print(f"{len(cells)} cells studied, {len(main)} cell-directions; responses found: {len(resp)} "
      f"in {int(cells.torque_related.sum())} cells")
flat = main[main.baseline_sd == 0]
print("Cell-directions without a usable baseline (SD of the baseline SDF 0; they can never respond):",
      len(flat), "| by type and state:", flat.groupby(["ptype", "state"]).size().to_dict())
print("Trials per cell and direction: ", main.n_trials.min(), "to", main.n_trials.max(),
      "| baseline rate range", round(cells.baseline_rate.min(), 2), "to", round(cells.baseline_rate.max(), 2), "spikes/s")
print("Response latencies (ms):", resp.latency.min(), "to", resp.latency.max(),
      "| offsets:", resp.offset.min(), "to", resp.offset.max())

# Per-cell results of the main detection, for recomputing any group statistic: baseline rate, and per
# direction the baseline SD of the mean SDF, the threshold half-width, and for a response its
# latency, sign and largest change.
t_main_ = stats.t.ppf(1 - stretch.P_THRESHOLD / 2, int(np.diff(stretch.BASELINE_MS)[0]) - 1)
per_cell = cells[["unit_name", "state", "ptype", "baseline_rate", "torque_related", "latency", "dsi", "category"]].copy()
for d, k in (("flexion", "F"), ("extension", "E")):
    x = main[main.direction == d].set_index("cell")
    per_cell[f"{k}_n"] = x.n_trials
    per_cell[f"{k}_thr"] = t_main_ * x.baseline_sd
    per_cell[f"{k}_lat"] = x.latency
    per_cell[f"{k}_sign"] = x.sign
    per_cell[f"{k}_max"] = x.max_change
print(per_cell.round(2).to_string())

cell-counts¶

In monkey V, 112 neurons were studied before MPTP and 159 after, of which 49 and 54 were PTNs and 31 and 48 CSNs; three neurons in all were activated from both the peduncle and the putamen.

In [13]:
counts = pd.crosstab(cells.ptype, cells.state).reindex(columns=["pre", "post"])
counts.loc["all"] = counts.sum()
print("Monkey V cells studied by type and state:")
print(counts.to_string())
dual_all = units[units.ptype == "dual"]
print(f"\nUnits activated from both the peduncle and the putamen, all files: {len(dual_all)} "
      f"({dual_all.subject.value_counts().to_dict()}); among the cells studied: {int((cells.ptype == 'dual').sum())}")
print("Other dual projections (with thalamus or STN):", int(units.projection.str.contains('_and_').sum() - len(dual_all)))
print("\nVariant, the two unit copies in repeated files dropped:")
print(pd.crosstab(cells[~cells.duplicate_copy].ptype, cells[~cells.duplicate_copy].state)
      .reindex(columns=["pre", "post"]).to_string())
# Units recorded across several source files are one cell in this version. Variant: each unit
# counted from the perturbations of its first source file only (the source_file of its first observed
# trial; a unit of a repeated "b" file has its trials stored under the earlier file's name).
first_only = []
for r in units.itertuples():
    u = S[r.si]["units"][r.ui]
    src = S[r.si]["trials"].source_file.values
    f0 = src[np.flatnonzero(u["observed_trials"])[0]]
    own = src[u["pert_trial"]] == f0
    d = u["pert_direction"][own]
    first_only.append(((d == "flexion").sum() >= stretch.MIN_REPS) & ((d == "extension").sum() >= stretch.MIN_REPS))
fo = units.assign(studied_first=first_only)
fo = fo[fo.studied_first & (fo.subject == "Venus")]
print("\nVariant, units across several files counted from their first file only:")
print(pd.crosstab(fo.ptype, fo.state).reindex(columns=["pre", "post"]).to_string())

Result: reproduced. The monkey V cells studied number 115 before and 157 after MPTP, with 51 and 54 PTNs and 32 and 48 CSNs, all within tolerance of the supplementary table's 112 and 159, 49 and 54, 31 and 48; the files hold 3 units activated from both the peduncle and the putamen, all in monkey V and all among the cells studied. Counting each unit from its first source file only (variant) gives 112 and 157, with 49 and 54 PTNs and 31 and 48 CSNs. The published version gave the table's counts exactly (112 and 159), counting the two unit copies the draft no longer holds and without the trials of the second files.

monkey-l-perturbations¶

In monkey L, 57 of 115 neurons before MPTP and 35 of 73 after responded to torque perturbations of the wrist.

Blocked: the monkey L files mark no torque perturbation (data check above; the type is not_available in every trial), so neither the trials nor their onsets can be found. The files hold 138 and 72 monkey L units, against the paper's 115 and 73 cells studied.

baseline-rate¶

Before torque onset, the firing rate of M1 neurons was lower after MPTP, because PTN rates fell (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001) while CSN rates did not change (p = 0.5). In monkey V, 12.6 and 8.9 spikes/s for all cells, 20.3 and 14.8 for PTNs, 3.5 and 3.4 for CSNs.

In [14]:
def mwu(a, b):
    return stats.mannwhitneyu(a, b, alternative="two-sided").pvalue


expected_rate = {"M1": (12.6, 8.9, 1.98, 1.33), "PTN": (20.3, 14.8, 2.46, 2.72), "CSN": (3.5, 3.4, 1.47, 1.01)}
rows = []
for g, (e_pre, e_post, t_pre, t_post) in expected_rate.items():
    sub = cells if g == "M1" else cells[cells.ptype == g]
    pre, post = sub[sub.state == "pre"].baseline_rate, sub[sub.state == "post"].baseline_rate
    rows.append({"group": g, "n_pre": len(pre), "pre": pre.mean(), "sd_pre": pre.std(), "expected_pre": e_pre,
                 "in_tol_pre": abs(pre.mean() - e_pre) <= t_pre, "n_post": len(post), "post": post.mean(),
                 "sd_post": post.std(), "expected_post": e_post, "in_tol_post": abs(post.mean() - e_post) <= t_post,
                 "change_%": 100 * (post.mean() / pre.mean() - 1), "mwu_p": mwu(pre, post)})
rate_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(rate_table.round(4).to_string(index=False))
nodup = cells[~cells.duplicate_copy]
p = nodup[nodup.ptype == "PTN"]
print(f"\nVariant without the unit copies, PTN: {p[p.state == 'pre'].baseline_rate.mean():.2f} and "
      f"{p[p.state == 'post'].baseline_rate.mean():.2f} spikes/s, p = {mwu(p[p.state == 'pre'].baseline_rate, p[p.state == 'post'].baseline_rate):.4f}")

   M1    115 12.6618 10.8980          12.6        True     157  8.8463   9.4447            8.9         True  -30.1340 0.0022
  PTN     51 18.4881  9.7849          20.3        True      54 14.3682  10.1503           14.8         True  -22.2842 0.0201

Result: reproduced. All six means are within tolerance (M1 12.66 and 8.85, PTN 18.49 and 14.37, CSN 3.48 and 3.36 spikes/s). The PTN rate is lower after MPTP (Mann-Whitney p = 0.020) and the CSN rate does not differ (p = 0.65); the M1 rate is lower (p = 0.0022). The statement's p < 0.001 for PTNs, from both monkeys, is not reached in monkey V alone.

ptn-faster-than-csn¶

Before MPTP, PTNs fired much faster than CSNs at rest (Mann-Whitney p < 0.001).

In [15]:
pre = cells[cells.state == "pre"]
ptn_pre, csn_pre = pre[pre.ptype == "PTN"].baseline_rate, pre[pre.ptype == "CSN"].baseline_rate
print(f"PTN {ptn_pre.mean():.2f} spikes/s (range {ptn_pre.min():.2f} to {ptn_pre.max():.2f}, n = {len(ptn_pre)}); "
      f"CSN {csn_pre.mean():.2f} (range {csn_pre.min():.2f} to {csn_pre.max():.2f}, n = {len(csn_pre)}); "
      f"Mann-Whitney p = {mwu(ptn_pre, csn_pre):.2e}")

PTN 18.49 spikes/s (range 2.56 to 48.96, n = 51); CSN 3.48 (range 0.00 to 20.73, n = 32); Mann-Whitney p = 6.33e-12
Paper (both monkeys): text 16.3 and 3.6, Table 1 18.3 and 3.2 spikes/s

Result: reproduced. Before MPTP, monkey V PTNs fire at 18.49 spikes/s and CSNs at 3.48 (Mann-Whitney p = 6.3e-12).

antidromic-latency¶

PTN antidromic latencies did not change after MPTP (1.9 ms, p = 0.9), while CSN latencies were longer (5.1 against 6.1 ms, p < 0.05/3).

In [16]:
def antidromic(df, label):
    rows = []
    for g, e in (("PTN", (1.9, 1.9, 0.22, 0.2)), ("CSN", (5.1, 6.1, 0.61, 0.89))):
        sub = df[df.ptype == g]
        a, b = sub[sub.state == "pre"].antidromic_latency_ms.dropna(), sub[sub.state == "post"].antidromic_latency_ms.dropna()
        rows.append({"cells": label, "group": g, "n_pre": len(a), "pre": a.mean(), "sd_pre": a.std(),
                     "in_tol_pre": abs(a.mean() - e[0]) <= e[2], "n_post": len(b), "post": b.mean(),
                     "sd_post": b.std(), "in_tol_post": abs(b.mean() - e[1]) <= e[3], "mwu_p": mwu(a, b)})
    return rows


leu_units = units[(units.subject == "Leu") & units.ptype.isin(["PTN", "CSN"])]
ad = pd.DataFrame(antidromic(cells, "monkey V studied")
                  + antidromic(pd.concat([cells, leu_units]), "variant: plus all monkey L units"))
print(ad.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("Antidromic latency range (ms), cells studied:", cells.antidromic_latency_ms.min(), "to",
      cells.antidromic_latency_ms.max(), "| NaN for", int(cells[cells.ptype.isin(['PTN', 'CSN'])].antidromic_latency_ms.isna().sum()), "PTNs and CSNs")
alpha = 0.05 / 3
for r in ad.itertuples():
    if r.group == "CSN":
        verdict = f"longer after MPTP and below 0.05/3 = {alpha:.4f}: {bool(r.post > r.pre and r.mwu_p < alpha)}"
    else:
        verdict = f"p >= 0.05 (no difference): {bool(r.mwu_p >= 0.05)}"
    print(f"{r.cells}, {r.group}: Mann-Whitney p = {r.mwu_p:.4f}; {verdict}")

Result: partially reproduced. The four means are within tolerance (PTN 1.92 and 1.86 ms, CSN 4.91 and 6.85 ms) and the PTN latency does not differ (p = 0.68). The CSN latency is longer after MPTP with p = 0.019, just above the paper's threshold of 0.05/3 = 0.0167, so the CSN test fails (printed above). With all monkey L PTNs and CSNs added (variant), p = 0.0072 for CSNs and 0.78 for PTNs, and the post-MPTP CSN mean (7.01 ms) is outside tolerance.

false-positive-rate¶

The detection threshold, p < 0.01 divided by 5 independent comparisons, holds the chance of a false response over the 200 ms epoch near 0.01.

# Variant null: unperturbed trials, at the time a torque usually comes (the session's median delay
# from center target to torque onset), so the epoch matches the true one but has no torque.

for c in cells.itertuples():
    s, u = S[c.si], S[c.si]["units"][c.ui]
    tr = s["trials"]
    delay = np.nanmedian(tr.onset - tr.center_on)
    t0 = (tr.center_on + delay)[(tr.torque == "none") & u["observed_trials"]].dropna().values
    if len(t0) < stretch.MIN_REPS:

    rel = [np.round((u["spikes"][(u["spikes"] >= t - 1.8) & (u["spikes"] < t + 0.7)] - t) * 1000) for t in t0]
    for method in ("mean", "trials"):

# Where the false crossings come from. (1) The pseudo-onset rate by baseline rate and by number of
# trials. (2) Stationary Poisson spike trains at each cell-direction's baseline rate, with its number
# of trials, through the same detection: no response exists, so every crossing is false.

# How the result changes with the threshold. The main detection crosses when the largest change over
# 0 to 200 ms exceeds t times the baseline SD of the mean SDF; the t that gives a pseudo-onset rate
# of 0.01 is read off the pseudo-onset distribution of that ratio and applied at the true onset.
z_pseudo = pm.max_abs_z.fillna(-np.inf).values
t_main = stats.t.ppf(1 - stretch.P_THRESHOLD / 2, int(np.diff(stretch.BASELINE_MS)[0]) - 1)
t_cal = float(np.quantile(z_pseudo, 0.99))
print(f"t of the main detection {t_main:.2f}; t giving a pseudo-onset rate of 0.01: {t_cal:.2f}")
cal_rows = []
for (cell, d), m in mean_sdf.items():
    for shift in (0, stretch.PSEUDO_ONSET_MS):
        q = stretch.detect(m[None, :], shift_ms=shift, tcrit=t_cal)
        cal_rows.append({"cell": cell, "direction": d, "pseudo": shift != 0, "responds": q["responds"],
                         "any_crossing_0_200": q["any_crossing_0_200"]})
cal = pd.DataFrame(cal_rows)
print(cal.groupby("pseudo")[["any_crossing_0_200", "responds"]].mean().round(4).to_string())
cal_cell = cal[~cal.pseudo].groupby("cell").responds.any()
first_overall = main.assign(early=main.first_crossing < stretch.ONSET_RANGE_MS[0])
print(f"\nDetected responses (main) with an earlier crossing at 0 to {stretch.ONSET_RANGE_MS[0] - 1} ms: "
      f"{int((first_overall.responds & first_overall.early).sum())} of {int(main.responds.sum())}")
fo_cell = first_overall.assign(r=first_overall.responds & ~first_overall.early).groupby("cell").r.any()
rows = []
for label, rel in (("main", cells.torque_related), ("calibrated threshold", cal_cell.reindex(cells.index)),
                   ("first crossing overall in 20 to 60 ms", fo_cell.reindex(cells.index))):

# Do the spike windows fall inside the trials? Spikes are stored only inside trials, so a window that
# starts before its trial's start is partly empty by construction. For every perturbation of the cells
# studied: time from the trial start to the torque onset, and the share of perturbations whose
# spike window (-1800 ms), pseudo baseline with the kernel's reach (-1500 ms), true baseline with the
# kernel's reach (-900 ms), and SDF end (+600 ms, against the trial stop) fall outside the trial.
lead, tail = [], []
for c in cells.itertuples():
    s, u = S[c.si], S[c.si]["units"][c.ui]
    tr = s["trials"].loc[u["pert_trial"]]
    lead.append((tr.onset - tr.start).values * 1000)
    tail.append((tr.stop - tr.onset).values * 1000)
lead, tail = np.concatenate(lead), np.concatenate(tail)
print(f"{len(lead)} cell-perturbations; onset minus trial start (ms), percentiles 0/1/5/50/100:",
      np.percentile(lead, [0, 1, 5, 50, 100]).round(0))
print("Trial stop minus onset (ms), percentiles 0/1/50:", np.percentile(tail, [0, 1, 50]).round(0))
for label, ms in (("spike window, -1800 ms", 1800), ("pseudo baseline with kernel, -1500 ms", 1500),
                  ("true baseline with kernel, -900 ms", 900)):
    print(f"  {label}: starts before the trial start in {np.mean(lead < ms):.2%}")
print(f"  SDF end, +600 ms: after the trial stop in {np.mean(tail < 600):.2%}")

Result: blocked (methods underspecified). With the detection fixed in the claims file, a threshold crossing in the 200 ms after a pseudo onset 600 ms before the torque occurs in 0.23 of the 544 cell-directions, against the 0.01 the paper's threshold implies; the t-test variant gives 0.46. Unperturbed trials at the usual torque time give 0.19 and 0.44. Stationary Poisson spike trains at each cell-direction's baseline rate give 0.21 and 0.48 with the seed of the earlier attempt, and 0.16 to 0.19 (main detection) with eight other seeds, so most of the excess comes from the detection procedure, not from activity in the hold period. The rate does not fall with baseline rate or number of trials (0.18 to 0.29 by baseline rate quartile, 0.21 to 0.26 by number of trials). A response with onset between 20 and 60 ms is found in 0.048 of the cell-directions at the pseudo onset and 0.047 on unperturbed trials, against 0.375 at the true onset, a ratio of 0.13. Fourteen cell-directions (10 of them CSNs) have a baseline SD of exactly 0 and can never respond. Near-silent cell-directions with a threshold of about 0 can respond, and add to the false positives: v5801.1 has a baseline rate of 0.00 spikes/s and an extension "response" at 30 ms. The spike windows lie inside their trials: every torque onset comes at least 2968 ms after its trial's start and 1516 ms before its stop, so no window (from -1800 to +600 ms) is cut by a trial boundary. Both rates are about 23 and 46 times the paper's, so the procedure here does not give the rate the paper states for its own: either it differs from the paper's in a way the Methods do not settle, or the paper's stated rate does not hold, and this analysis cannot tell which. The claims that rest on the selection of responses are blocked with the same reason. A threshold calibrated to a pseudo-onset rate of 0.01 (t = 6.67 against 3.11) finds 30.4% and 32.5% of M1 cells torque-related, further from the paper's 75% and 68%; taking the first crossing anywhere in 0 to 200 ms as the onset removes 5 of the 204 responses. The analyses of the blocked claims are run below all the same, and their numbers are reported.

torque-related-fractions¶

In monkey V, 84 of 112 M1 neurons (75%) were torque-related before MPTP and 108 of 159 (68%) after; PTNs 27 of 49 (55%) and 37 of 54 (68%); CSNs 14 of 31 (45%) and 10 of 48 (21%).

                 ("CSN", "pre"): 45, ("CSN", "post"): 21}


def related_table(df, label):
    rows = []
    for (g, st), e in expected_frac.items():
        sub = df if g == "M1" else df[df.ptype == g]
        sub = sub[sub.state == st]
        k, n = int(sub.torque_related.sum()), len(sub)
        rows.append({"detection": label, "group": g, "state": st, "related": k, "n": n,
                     "percent": 100 * k / n, "expected": e, "in_tol": abs(100 * k / n - e) <= 0.1 * e})
    return rows

                          + related_table(cells.assign(torque_related=cells.torque_related_trials), "t-test variant")
                          + related_table(cells[~cells.duplicate_copy], "main, unit copies dropped"))
print(frac_table.round(1).to_string(index=False))

prevalence-unchanged¶

MPTP did not change the fraction of torque-related neurons, in M1, in PTNs or in CSNs (chi-square, p > 0.05/3).

In [23]:
def chi2_yates(a_k, a_n, b_k, b_n):
    table = np.array([[a_k, a_n - a_k], [b_k, b_n - b_k]])
    chi2, p, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(table, correction=True)
    return chi2, p


rows = []
for label, col in (("main", "torque_related"), ("t-test variant", "torque_related_trials")):
    for g in ("M1", "PTN", "CSN"):
        sub = cells if g == "M1" else cells[cells.ptype == g]
        a, b = sub[sub.state == "pre"][col], sub[sub.state == "post"][col]
        chi2, p = chi2_yates(a.sum(), len(a), b.sum(), len(b))
        rows.append({"detection": label, "group": g, "pre_%": 100 * a.mean(), "post_%": 100 * b.mean(),
                     "change_points": 100 * (b.mean() - a.mean()), "chi2": chi2, "p": p, "p_below_0.05/3": p < 0.05 / 3})
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("\nThe paper's monkey V counts, through the same test:",
      {g: round(chi2_yates(*k)[1], 4) for g, k in {"M1": (84, 112, 108, 159), "PTN": (27, 49, 37, 54), "CSN": (14, 31, 10, 48)}.items()})

ptn-more-responsive¶

PTNs responded to torque more often than CSNs (68% against 31%, chi-square 32.3, p < 0.001).

PTNs respond more often than CSNs (70.5% against 16.2%, chi-square 51.4, p = 7.4e-13); both fractions are outside tolerance, the PTN fraction above the expected 62.1 +/- 6.2% and the CSN fraction below the expected 30.4 +/- 3.0%. The t-test variant gives 61.9% and 35.0% (p = 5.1e-4).

About half of the torque-related cells (124 of 284, 44%) responded to only one direction.

      f"({100 * one.mean():.1f}%); by state: {tr_cells.groupby('state').apply(lambda d: round(100 * (d.n_directions == 1).mean(), 1)).to_dict()}")
vt = cells[cells.torque_related_trials]
n_dir_t = var["responds"].sum(axis=1).values[cells.torque_related_trials.values]
print(f"t-test variant: {int((n_dir_t == 1).sum())}/{len(vt)} ({100 * (n_dir_t == 1).mean():.1f}%)")

Torque-related cells responding in one direction only: 72/138 (52.2%); by state: {'post': 46.7, 'pre': 58.7}
t-test variant: 92/143 (64.3%)

Result: blocked (methods underspecified), as the selection of responses is (see false-positive-rate). 52.2% of torque-related cells (72 of 138) respond to one direction only (58.7% before MPTP, 46.7% after), against the expected 44 +/- 4.4%; the t-test variant gives 64.3%.

excitatory-majority¶

Most torque responses were increases in firing (86% and 88% of M1 responses; 70% and 75% for PTNs), and MPTP did not change the PTN balance (chi-square 0.1, p = 0.7).

In [26]:
rows = []
for g in ("M1", "PTN", "CSN"):
    sub = resp if g == "M1" else resp[resp.ptype == g]
    for st in ("pre", "post"):
        x = sub[sub.state == st]
        rows.append({"group": g, "state": st, "increases": int((x.sign > 0).sum()), "responses": len(x),
                     "percent": 100 * (x.sign > 0).mean(),
                     "flexion": f"{int(((x.sign > 0) & (x.direction == 'flexion')).sum())}/{int((x.direction == 'flexion').sum())}",
                     "extension": f"{int(((x.sign > 0) & (x.direction == 'extension')).sum())}/{int((x.direction == 'extension').sum())}"})
inc = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(inc.round(1).to_string(index=False))
for g in ("PTN", "CSN"):
    a, b = inc[(inc.group == g) & (inc.state == "pre")].iloc[0], inc[(inc.group == g) & (inc.state == "post")].iloc[0]
    chi2, p = chi2_yates(a.increases, a.responses, b.increases, b.responses)
    print(f"{g} increases pre against post: chi-square {chi2:.2f}, p = {p:.3f}")
print("All responses, both states:", f"{100 * (resp.sign > 0).mean():.1f}% increases of {len(resp)}")
chi2, p = chi2_yates(23, 24, 19, 22)
print(f"Reference, the paper's own CSN counts in Table 1 (23/24 against 19/22): chi-square {chi2:.2f}, p = {p:.2f} "

The paper's Table 1 marks its CSN change p < 0.01, but its own counts give p = 0.54 with the test it names.

magnitude-unchanged and venus-response-magnitudes¶

The magnitude of torque responses did not differ before and after MPTP, for M1 cells or for PTNs, by any of three measures (Kolmogorov-Smirnov and Mann-Whitney, all p > 0.15).

In monkey V the mean response magnitudes were 42.4 and 37.9 spikes/s (M1 flexion), 50.9 and 42.6 (M1 extension), 33.4 and 26.1 (PTN flexion), 38.8 and 29.3 (PTN extension).

latency-shorter¶

Response latencies were shorter after MPTP for M1 cells and for PTNs, for flexion and extension (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, all p < 0.05). Monkey V means 39.2 and 34.6 ms (M1 flexion), 40.4 and 33.4 (M1 extension), 43.9 and 35.5 (PTN flexion), 44.4 and 36.7 (PTN extension).

In [29]:
expected_lat = {("M1", "flexion"): (39.2, 34.56), ("M1", "extension"): (40.4, 33.4),
                ("PTN", "flexion"): (43.9, 35.5), ("PTN", "extension"): (44.4, 36.7)}


def latency_table(rsp):
    rows = []
    for (g, d), (e_pre, e_post) in expected_lat.items():
        sub = rsp if g == "M1" else rsp[rsp.ptype == g]
        x = sub[sub.direction == d]
        a, b = x[x.state == "pre"].latency, x[x.state == "post"].latency
        rows.append({"group": g, "direction": d, "n_pre": len(a), "pre": a.mean(), "expected_pre": e_pre,
                     "in_tol_pre": abs(a.mean() - e_pre) <= 0.1 * e_pre, "n_post": len(b), "post": b.mean(),
                     "expected_post": e_post, "in_tol_post": abs(b.mean() - e_post) <= 0.1 * e_post,
                     "ks_p": stats.ks_2samp(a, b).pvalue, "mwu_p": mwu(a, b)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)


lat = latency_table(resp)
print(lat.round(4).to_string(index=False))
print("\nPooled means (paper, both monkeys: M1 41 and 35 ms, PTN 46 and 38 ms):")

    print(f"  {g}: responses {sub[sub.state == 'pre'].latency.mean():.1f} and {sub[sub.state == 'post'].latency.mean():.1f} ms; "
          f"earliest per cell {cs[cs.state == 'pre'].latency.mean():.1f} and {cs[cs.state == 'post'].latency.mean():.1f} ms "
          f"(KS p = {stats.ks_2samp(cs[cs.state == 'pre'].latency, cs[cs.state == 'post'].latency).pvalue:.4f})")

latency-not-training¶

Latencies did not correlate with the days of training (monkey V Spearman |rho| = 0.02, p = 0.85).

In [30]:
tr_cells = cells[cells.torque_related].copy()
first_day = sessions[sessions.subject == "Venus"].date.min()
tr_cells["day"] = (tr_cells.date - first_day).dt.days
rho, p = stats.spearmanr(tr_cells.day, tr_cells.latency)
print(f"All torque-related cells (n = {len(tr_cells)}): Spearman rho = {rho:.3f}, p = {p:.4f}; days {tr_cells.day.min()} to {tr_cells.day.max()}")
for st in ("pre", "post"):
    x = tr_cells[tr_cells.state == st]
    rho, p = stats.spearmanr(x.day, x.latency)
    print(f"  {st}: n = {len(x)}, rho = {rho:.3f}, p = {p:.4f}")

All torque-related cells (n = 138): Spearman rho = -0.249, p = 0.0033; days 0 to 360
  pre: n = 63, rho = 0.084, p = 0.5106
  post: n = 75, rho = -0.147, p = 0.2083

Result: blocked (methods underspecified), as the selection of responses is (see false-positive-rate). Latency correlates with the day of recording over both states (rho = -0.25, p = 0.0033, n = 138), as post-MPTP sessions come later; within each state it does not (p = 0.51 and 0.21).

fwhm-shorter-ptn¶

Torque-evoked increases in PTN firing were briefer after MPTP (FWHM 73 to 50 ms over both monkeys; Mann-Whitney p < 0.05 for each direction). Monkey V: 97 and 52 ms (flexion), 57 and 41 ms (extension).

dsi-reduced, venus-dsi and dsi-not-baseline¶

Directional selectivity fell after MPTP; reciprocal and unidirectional responses became less common (chi-square 22.2, p < 0.001).

In monkey V the mean DSI was 0.72 and 0.66 (M1), 0.73 and 0.75 (PTN), 0.81 and 0.83 (CSN).

Pre-torque rates did not differ between directional categories (one-way ANOVA, F = 0.77, p = 0.46).

In [32]:
cats = ["reciprocal", "unidirectional", "bidirectional", "non-directional"]
tr_cells = cells[cells.torque_related]
tab = pd.crosstab(tr_cells.category, tr_cells.state).reindex(index=cats, columns=["pre", "post"]).fillna(0)
print(tab.to_string())
chi2, p, dof, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(tab.values)
high = tr_cells.category.isin(["reciprocal", "unidirectional"])
fr = high.groupby(tr_cells.state).mean()
print(f"\nReciprocal or unidirectional: pre {100 * fr['pre']:.1f}%, post {100 * fr['post']:.1f}% "
      f"(change {100 * (fr['post'] - fr['pre']):.1f} points); chi-square (2 x 4) {chi2:.2f}, dof {dof}, p = {p:.4f}")
for g in ("PTN", "CSN"):
    x = tr_cells[tr_cells.ptype == g]
    t = pd.crosstab(x.category, x.state).reindex(index=cats, columns=["pre", "post"]).fillna(0)
    t = t[t.sum(axis=1) > 0]
    c2, pp, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(t.values)
    h = x.category.isin(["reciprocal", "unidirectional"]).groupby(x.state).mean()
    print(f"  {g}: reciprocal or unidirectional pre {100 * h.get('pre', np.nan):.1f}%, post {100 * h.get('post', np.nan):.1f}%; chi-square p = {pp:.3f}")

# Variant: categories from the DSI value as the paper words them: reciprocal DSI > 1, unidirectional
# a response in one direction only (DSI <= 1), bidirectional 0.5 < DSI <= 1, non-directional DSI <= 0.5.
def by_value(r):
    if r.dsi > 1:
        return "reciprocal"
    if r.n_directions == 1:
        return "unidirectional"
    return "bidirectional" if r.dsi > 0.5 else "non-directional"


tr_v = tr_cells.assign(category_value=[by_value(r) for r in tr_cells.itertuples()])
tab_v = pd.crosstab(tr_v.category_value, tr_v.state).reindex(index=cats, columns=["pre", "post"]).fillna(0)
chi2_v, p_v, _, _ = stats.chi2_contingency(tab_v.values)
fr_v = tr_v.category_value.isin(["reciprocal", "unidirectional"]).groupby(tr_v.state).mean()
print("\nVariant, categories by DSI value:")
print(tab_v.to_string())
print(f"Reciprocal or unidirectional: pre {100 * fr_v['pre']:.1f}%, post {100 * fr_v['post']:.1f}%; chi-square {chi2_v:.2f}, p = {p_v:.4f}")
print("Smallest expected count in the main 2 x 4 table:", round(stats.chi2_contingency(tab.values)[3].min(), 1))

Reciprocal and unidirectional cells fall from 58.7% to 52.0% of torque-related cells, by 6.7 points, without significance (chi-square 5.70, p = 0.13). With categories set from the DSI value as the paper words them (reciprocal above 1), the fraction falls from 61.9% to 50.7% (p = 0.36). The main table has no reciprocal cell before MPTP; its smallest expected count is 1.8, so the chi-square p is approximate. The DSI's P and NP are the largest changes over 0 to 200 ms, whether or not a response was detected there, a choice made here.

Kinematics and EMG¶

Session measures use monkey V files with analog data. No file repeats another's recording in this version, so none is left out (in the published version four were). Kinematics are measured on every perturbation; a trial whose joint was already moving faster than 5 deg/s in the 50 ms before onset is counted and kept.

In [35]:
# Per-trial torque command step, in multiples of the smallest session level (as in the data check)
level_unit = command.step[command.step > 10].min()
trial_level = {}
for s in venus:
    w = s["windows"]["torque_cmd"]
    sign = np.where(s["pert_direction"] == "flexion", 1.0, -1.0)
    rel = (w - np.nanmedian(w[:, (AX >= -100) & (AX < 0)], axis=1, keepdims=True)) * sign[:, None]
    trial_level[s["session_id"].split("++")[1]] = np.round(np.nanmedian(rel[:, (AX >= 10) & (AX < 40)], axis=1) / level_unit)
kin_rows = []
for s in venus:
    if s["session_id"].split("++")[1] in repeated_files:
        continue
    tl = trial_level[s["session_id"].split("++")[1]]
    for k, d in enumerate(s["pert_direction"]):
        r = stretch.kinematics(s["windows"]["angle"][k], d, s["analog_step_ms"])
        if r["valid"]:
            kin_rows.append({"session": s["session_id"], "post": s["post"], "direction": d,
                             "trial_level": tl[k], **r})
kin = pd.DataFrame(kin_rows)
kin["state"] = np.where(kin.post, "post", "pre")
print(f"{len(kin)} perturbations in {kin.session.nunique()} sessions; moving before onset: {int(kin.moving_before.sum())}; "
      f"no velocity crossing within 150 ms: {int(kin.latency_ms.isna().sum())}")
print("Ranges: latency", kin.latency_ms.min(), "to", kin.latency_ms.max(), "ms; peak velocity",
      round(kin.peak_velocity.min(), 1), "to", round(kin.peak_velocity.max(), 1), "deg/s; amplitude",
      round(kin.amplitude.min(), 2), "to", round(kin.amplitude.max(), 2), "deg")
sess_kin = kin.groupby(["session", "state", "direction"])[["latency_ms", "peak_velocity", "amplitude"]].mean().reset_index()
sess_kin["level"] = sess_kin.session.map(command.set_index("session").level)
print("\nSession means, mean over sessions:")
print(sess_kin.groupby(["direction", "state"])[["latency_ms", "peak_velocity", "amplitude"]].agg(["mean", "count"]).round(2).to_string())

kinematics-slower¶

After MPTP, torque-induced displacements were slower and smaller; mean peak velocity fell by 16.2% and amplitude by 6.6% (ANOVA, F > 515 and F > 49).

In [36]:
def anova(df, measure):
    model = ols(f"{measure} ~ C(state) * C(direction)", data=df).fit()
    return sm.stats.anova_lm(model, typ=2)

Result: not reproduced. In monkey V, torque-induced movements are faster and larger after MPTP: session-mean peak velocity rises by 28.1% and amplitude by 14.6% over both directions (29.7% and 11.4% for flexion), with MPTP effects F = 98.6 and 24.1 (p < 0.0001). Restricted to the sessions with the same torque command size (variant), the increase is larger (98.2% and 109.0%). The mean of the session-mean peak velocities is 59.0 deg/s, and only one response comes from a session in the paper's 130 to 200 deg/s window of matched sessions. The angle's scale matches the files' own kinematic columns (data check), so the small torque-induced movements (mean amplitude 3.10 deg, where the paper gives a mean of 10 deg) are in the data and do not come from the measure here. Compared trial by trial at the same command step (variant), the result is mixed: at twice the smallest step, flexion movements are faster and larger after MPTP (median peak velocity 31.5 against 112.4 deg/s, p < 0.0001), extension movements do not differ (p = 0.37 and 0.20), at the smallest step extension movements are slower and smaller after MPTP (43.6 against 13.7 deg/s, 36 post-MPTP trials), and at four times the smallest step extension peak velocity does not differ (p = 0.46, 24 pre-MPTP trials from 4 sessions). The torque command differs between the states, so the change cannot be attributed to MPTP.

kinematic-latency-unchanged¶

The latency of torque-induced displacements did not change after MPTP (F < 0.2, p > 0.05).

# The zero-phase filter on synthetic movements: the angle is flat, then moves from a known time at
# a constant velocity (a ramp), or follows a 50 ms smooth pulse. The latency each measure reports
# against the true start shows how far the forwards-backwards FIR moves an onset earlier.
ax_ = np.arange(stretch.ANALOG_WINDOW_MS[0], stretch.ANALOG_WINDOW_MS[1] + 1)
rows = []
for shape in ("ramp", "smooth pulse"):
    for start in (5, 10, 20, 40):
        for vel in (20, 60, 200):          # deg/s
            t = np.clip(ax_ - start, 0, None) / 1000
            if shape == "ramp":
                ang = vel * t
            else:                          # velocity rises and falls over 50 ms (raised cosine), then holds
                v = np.where((t > 0) & (t < 0.05), vel * (1 - np.cos(2 * np.pi * t / 0.05)) / 2, 0.0)
                ang = np.cumsum(v) / 1000
            r = stretch.kinematics(ang, "flexion", 1)
            rows.append({"shape": shape, "true_start_ms": start, "velocity": vel, "latency_filtered": r["latency_ms"],
                         "latency_causal": r["latency_causal_ms"], "moving_before": r["moving_before"]})
syn = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(syn.to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nFiltered latency minus true start: {(syn.latency_filtered - syn.true_start_ms).min():.0f} to "
      f"{(syn.latency_filtered - syn.true_start_ms).max():.0f} ms; causal: {(syn.latency_causal - syn.true_start_ms).min():.0f} "
      f"to {(syn.latency_causal - syn.true_start_ms).max():.0f} ms; flagged moving before onset: {int(syn.moving_before.sum())} of {len(syn)}")

                     "pre": x.mean(), "post": y.mean(), "mwu_p": mwu(x, y)})

Result: not reproduced. The movement onset latency is shorter after MPTP (session means 9.65 and 3.05 ms for flexion, 10.86 and 5.82 ms for extension; MPTP F = 1037, p < 0.0001), with an MPTP by direction interaction (F = 18.5). In the sessions with the same command size (variant) it does not differ (7.68 and 7.62 ms, p = 0.83). The zero-phase filter can move an onset earlier, and 241 of 5550 perturbations have a latency of 0 ms. With a causal 10 ms average of the unfiltered velocity, which cannot move it earlier, the session means are 12.5 to 18.5 ms and still shorter after MPTP (F = 791); leaving out the trials already moving before onset gives F = 1043 (filtered) and 762 (causal). At the middle command size the causal variant gives p = 0.25, and p = 0.025 without the trials moving before onset. On synthetic movements the filtered latency is 14 ms early to 5 ms late against the true start, and the causal one 1 to 13 ms late; 9 of 24 synthetic movements that start after the onset are flagged as moving before it. Compared trial by trial at the same command step (variant), latencies are not shorter after MPTP: at twice the smallest step, flexion 7.17 and 7.17 ms (p = 0.96) and extension 7.99 and 9.00 ms (p = 0.0023), and the causal measure is longer after MPTP in both directions (p <= 0.0001, differences under 1 ms). The latency difference goes with the torque command, so it cannot be attributed to MPTP; the outcome is the criterion's comparison.

EMG¶

Session-average responses of the three triceps channels to flexion torques, which stretch the triceps, with the extension torques shown for the contrast.

In [40]:
emg_rows, traces = [], {}
for s in venus:
    code_ = s["session_id"].split("++")[1]
    if code_ in repeated_files:
        continue
    for ch in stretch.EMG_CHANNELS[:3]:
        if ch not in s["windows"]:
            continue
        w = s["windows"][ch]
        if np.isnan(w).any() or np.nanstd(w[:, AX < 0]) < 1:
            continue
        for d in ("flexion", "extension"):
            r = stretch.emg_response(w[s["pert_direction"] == d], s["analog_step_ms"])
            emg_rows.append({"session": code_, "post": s["post"], "channel": ch, "direction": d,
                             **{k: r[k] for k in ("m1", "m2", "onset_ms", "duration_ms")}})
            traces[(code_, ch, d)] = r["trace"]
emg = pd.DataFrame(emg_rows)
emg["state"] = np.where(emg.post, "post", "pre")
emg["level"] = emg.session.map(command.set_index("code").level)

# Variant: pre against post at the same per-trial command step. Session averages are rebuilt from the
# flexion perturbations of one per-trial level only (at least 5 in the session), so pre and post
# traces come from the same command step.
lvl_rows = []
for s in venus:
    code_ = s["session_id"].split("++")[1]
    if code_ in repeated_files:
        continue
    tl = trial_level[code_]
    for ch in stretch.EMG_CHANNELS[:3]:
        if ch not in s["windows"]:
            continue
        w = s["windows"][ch]
        if np.isnan(w).any() or np.nanstd(w[:, AX < 0]) < 1:
            continue
        for lv in np.unique(tl[np.isfinite(tl)]):
            k = (s["pert_direction"] == "flexion") & (tl == lv)
            if k.sum() < stretch.MIN_REPS:
                continue
            r = stretch.emg_response(w[k], s["analog_step_ms"])
            lvl_rows.append({"session": code_, "state": "post" if s["post"] else "pre", "channel": ch,
                             "trial_level": int(lv), "n_trials": int(k.sum()),
                             **{q: r[q] for q in ("m1", "m2", "onset_ms", "duration_ms")}})
emg_lvl = pd.DataFrame(lvl_rows)
print("Channel-sessions with at least 5 flexion perturbations of one per-trial level, by level and state:")
print(pd.crosstab(emg_lvl.trial_level, emg_lvl.state).reindex(columns=["pre", "post"]).fillna(0).astype(int).to_string())
rows = []
for lv, g in emg_lvl.groupby("trial_level"):
    a, b = g[g.state == "pre"], g[g.state == "post"]
    if len(a) < 5 or len(b) < 5:
        continue
    for ch in stretch.EMG_CHANNELS[:3] + ("all triceps",):
        x, y = (a, b) if ch == "all triceps" else (a[a.channel == ch], b[b.channel == ch])
        if len(x) < 3 or len(y) < 3:
            continue
        xd, yd = x.dropna(subset=["duration_ms"]), y.dropna(subset=["duration_ms"])
        rows.append({"level": lv, "channel": ch, "n_pre": len(x), "n_post": len(y),
                     "m2_pre": x.m2.median(), "m2_post": y.m2.median(), "m2_ks_p": stats.ks_2samp(x.m2, y.m2).pvalue,
                     "dur_pre": xd.duration_ms.mean(), "dur_post": yd.duration_ms.mean(),
                     "dur_ks_p": stats.ks_2samp(xd.duration_ms, yd.duration_ms).pvalue if len(xd) > 1 and len(yd) > 1 else np.nan,
                     "onset_pre": xd.onset_ms.mean(), "onset_post": yd.onset_ms.mean(),
                     "onset_ks_p": stats.ks_2samp(xd.onset_ms, yd.onset_ms).pvalue if len(xd) > 1 and len(yd) > 1 else np.nan})
print("\nPre against post at the same per-trial level (levels with at least 5 channel-sessions in each state;"
      " m2 medians in A/D units, duration and onset means in ms):")
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3).to_string(index=False))

Result: reproduced. For flexion torques, the m2 response is larger after MPTP in all three triceps channels (medians 3.1 against 164.0, 3.7 against 297.1 and 5.5 against 76.0 A/D units; Kolmogorov-Smirnov p < 1e-14 for each). The increase follows the torque command: in sessions of the middle command size (variant), m2 is not larger after MPTP on triceps longus 1 (median 47.6 against 1.3, p = 0.013, in the opposite direction). By command size and state the median m2 is 0.86 at the smallest size (pre only), 41.85 (pre) and 1.81 (post) at the middle, and 17.09 (pre, n = 5) and 194.4 (post) at the largest, so before MPTP it does not rise with command size (the largest size has only 5 channel-sessions), while after MPTP it rises from 1.81 at the middle size to 194.4 at the largest. Rebuilt from the perturbations of one per-trial command step (variant), at twice the smallest step the median m2 over the triceps channels is 44.9 before and 1.8 after MPTP (Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 0.004, 66 and 11 channel-sessions), though on triceps longus 2 it is larger after MPTP (52.2 against 113.0, n = 26 and 4, p = 0.36); no other step has 5 channel-sessions in both states. As the torque command is about four times larger in most post-MPTP sessions, the increase cannot be attributed to MPTP; the outcome is the criterion's comparison.

emg-duration-longer and emg-onset-unchanged¶

The total duration of EMG responses to torque increased after MPTP, from 57 +/- 6 to 79 +/- 3 ms (Kolmogorov-Smirnov, p < 0.001). The latency of the earliest EMG responses did not change.

Result: partially reproduced. EMG responses last longer after MPTP (24.6 against 49.4 ms, Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 4.1e-36), but both means are outside tolerance (expected 57 and 79 ms); thresholds of 1.5 and 3 SD give the same direction (20.8 against 50.1 and 23.4 against 50.1 ms; responses that last to the end of the window are now kept in these variants, as in the main one, where 5 of 560 do). At the middle command size (variant) the durations do not differ (29.2 and 27.9 ms, p = 0.94). Before MPTP 63.4% of the durations are 10 ms or less (median 9 ms, against 59 ms after), so many pre-MPTP responses are brief crossings of a small signal. At the same per-trial command step (twice the smallest, variant) the durations do not differ (33.5 and 22.2 ms, p = 0.43).

Result: not reproduced. The onset of the EMG response is earlier after MPTP (40.3 against 24.0 ms, Kolmogorov-Smirnov p = 9.1e-21), with the same direction at thresholds of 1.5 and 3 SD. At the middle command size (variant) the onsets do not differ (28.8 and 45.5 ms, p = 0.18), the post-MPTP onset being the later one there; at the same per-trial command step it is also later after MPTP (28.5 and 48.6 ms, p = 0.087).

emg-m1-weak¶

The short-latency m1 component (15 to 40 ms) was poorly formed and generally much smaller than m2.

velocity-matched-magnitude¶

In sessions with equivalent torque-induced velocities (130 to 200 deg/s), MPTP did not change the magnitude of responses (Mann-Whitney, p = 0.19 and 0.46; 24 and 33 flexion, 22 and 31 extension responses).

session-correlations¶

Across sessions, the mean PTN latency did not correlate with peak velocity (|rho| < 0.18) or with the m2 EMG response (|rho| < 0.26; Spearman, threshold 0.05/4).

        r2, p2 = stats.spearmanr(sub.latency, sub[col])
        print(f"   {'post' if st else 'pre'} only: rho = {r2:.3f}, p = {p2:.4f} (n = {len(sub)})")

Result: blocked (methods underspecified), as the selection of responses is (see false-positive-rate). Over 70 sessions, mean PTN latency does not reach the paper's threshold with velocity (rho = -0.16, p = 0.19) or with the triceps longus 1 m2 (rho = -0.28, p = 0.023, n = 67, above 0.0125); within each state neither correlates (p 0.37 to 0.87).

trial-correlations¶

Trial by trial, PTN response latencies did not correlate with the peak velocity or the m2 EMG response (Spearman |rho| < 0.34, p > 0.05).

Blocked: the Methods define response onset on the trial-averaged SDF and give no way of measuring a latency on a single trial, which this test needs.

Summary¶

A failure to reproduce here may be a failure of this attempt, not of the paper: see the reasoning and the differences from the paper's method.
